before_faq: Encaustic is a wax-based painting technique, from the Greek enkaustikos, meaning \"burned in,\" in which pigment is bound in melted beeswax and applied while warm, often reworked afterward using heated implements to build up thick, textured brushwork. Tempera, in the context of ancient painting, refers instead to a water-based binder, commonly egg or animal glue, applied cold in fine, hatched strokes. The distinction sounds clean in theory; the Getty Museum's 2020 analysis of the pair discussed above identified beeswax as the dominant binder in each, even though one has the flat, matte surface long treated as tempera's visual signature.

Punic wax is a specially prepared form of beeswax that Pliny the Elder, writing in the first century AD, placed at the top of his ranking of wax grades, describing a bleaching process of repeated boiling in seawater with nitre. Pliny's passage sits within a section on garlands and general wax preparation, not painting specifically, and scholars disagree on what it describes, some reading it as basic purification, others as a form of chemical saponification of the wax. No chemical study of an actual mummy portrait has yet confirmed that either version of Punic wax, or any of the specific recipes built on it since the 1890s, was the medium the Fayum painters actually used.

Roughly 900 of these portraits are known, painted on wood panels and bound into the wrappings of mummies from Roman Egypt; they are almost entirely unsigned, and no individual portrait painter is documented by name in the surviving ancient sources. Per Wikipedia's summary of the current scholarly consensus, they date from the late 1st century BC or early 1st century AD through roughly the middle of the 3rd century AD, with the pair examined in the Getty Museum's 2020 study, discussed above, dated more specifically to the early-to-mid-2nd century AD.

No. He said so directly, writing that nobody had settled who first painted in wax or devised encaustic designs. He recorded competing claims, that Aristides discovered it and Praxiteles perfected it, against evidence of still-earlier encaustic work by other named painters. Pliny does credit Pausias, introduced above, as the painter whose reputation in the medium outlasted his rivals, but that is a claim about renown, not invention.

Yes. In 1840, Duke Carlo Lodovico of Lucca commissioned a restoration of the church of Sant'Alessandro in Lucca, directed by the architect Lorenzo Nottolini, and the Italian painter Michele Ridolfi was hired to render its apse in hot wax, the same burned-in method covered throughout this page. It's one of the clearest documented cases of the 19th-century European revival, predating the 1893 Chicago recipe discussed above, though nobody appears to have published lab testing of Ridolfi's apse paintings confirming exactly which wax formula he used.

before_faq: It covers wall paintings and illuminated manuscripts from around 1000 to 1200 CE, made across Europe and surviving today mainly in curved church apses and in manuscript collections. It draws heavily on Byzantine models, favoring stiff, front-facing figures, drapery picked out in flat outlined colour, and a limited, deliberately layered palette, visible in the Pyrenees apse fresco discussed above, where the blue pigment derives from aerinite over a black base, and the red from cinnabar layered over haematite. Christ in Majesty, shown enthroned within an almond-shaped mandorla and ringed by four evangelists' symbols, is one of the period's most common subjects.

Specialist Italian restorers such as Franco Steffanoni used a method known as strappo, which made it possible to detach a fresco's paint layer from its wall in one continuous sheet, for the first time at scale, right as international demand for early medieval art was rising. Remote rural churches in Spain's Pyrenees and Castile had little practical protection even after national governments began formally designating them historic monuments starting in 1917, since that designation didn't retroactively stop an already-legal private sale. Whether a specific church's murals stayed together in a museum collection or scattered to private buyers usually depended on which side, a national museum or an art dealer, reached the church and its rector first.

In July 1926, two dozen mural panels were removed from the hermitage using strappo and sold through a dealer network operating out of Barcelona. Twenty-three made it to New York; the last one's whereabouts remain unknown to this day. Those that arrived were divided among several North American museums, named in the paragraph above, with six scenes later transferred to the Prado Museum in Madrid under a long-term loan, part of a 1957 exchange for an unrelated church apse.

No. The original apse fresco was removed between 1919 and 1923 and is on display in Barcelona today, at the museum introduced above as MNAC, about 300 kilometers away. A precise plaster cast has stood in the church's apse in its place since the removal, so a visitor sees the original composition and colours, but not the twelfth-century paint itself, unless they make the trip to Barcelona.

before_faq: It works by sending infrared wavelengths through a panel or canvas's paint film. Most paint is more transparent to infrared light than to visible light, while the carbon-based materials artists used for underdrawing, such as charcoal, absorb it strongly, so a reflectogram captures the hidden drawing as a distinct pattern. London's National Gallery used the technique in 2004/05 to uncover an entirely different composition hidden beneath one of Leonardo's paintings, detailed below.

Two underdrawings lie beneath the composition on display today, according to the museum's research. The first is a wholly different design that was never painted; a 2019 investigation combining XRF elemental mapping with hyperspectral scans recovered its design for the angel and Christ child, both positioned well above where they sit in the work now on view. The other underdrawing is closer to the final composition but still shows changes, including a shift in the pose of the Christ child's head.

An underdrawing is evidence that a detail was part of a painter's plan from the start. A National Gallery bulletin from 1995, covering the double portrait discussed above, identified details around the room's wall mirror, long assumed essential to what the picture symbolizes, as additions made late in the process with no preparatory sketch beneath them, meaning the imaging can date when a detail was added even though it cannot settle what that detail was meant to mean.

Leonardo departed for Milan from Florence in 1482, midway through the commission, according to the Uffizi, the Florence museum that now holds the panel. Its published account of the panel's restoration, carried out between 2011 and 2017, describes changed, layered passages rather than one settled design, with some areas still only at the drawing stage.

Fresco cartoons from this period rarely survived the transfer: perforated along their outlines and pounced with charcoal dust to stencil the design onto wet plaster. This one survived instead. The Milan library holding it since 1610 calls it the largest surviving cartoon of its kind, measuring 295.1×813.8 cm. Set against the completed wall painting, the cartoon lacks the architectural backdrop and two figures, one of them Raphael's own likeness, both entered into the design only after the cartoon stage.

Art historians commonly divide the period into four phases: the Proto-Renaissance (roughly the 1300s, associated with Giotto), the Early Renaissance (much of the 1400s, associated with Botticelli and Donatello), the High Renaissance (roughly 1495 to 1520, associated with Leonardo, Michelangelo, and Raphael), and the Northern Renaissance, the parallel movement in the Low Countries and Germany associated with painters like Jan van Eyck and Albrecht Dürer.

The five names that come up most consistently are Leonardo, Michelangelo, Raphael, Sandro Botticelli, and Titian. Leonardo, Michelangelo, and Raphael are usually grouped together as the High Renaissance's central figures; Botticelli belongs to the earlier Florentine Renaissance, and Titian led the later Venetian school.

The period produced some of the most reproduced images in Western art: Da Vinci's Mona Lisa and his The Last Supper, Michelangelo's [Sistine Chapel ceiling](/michelangelo-sistine-chapel/) and his sculpture David, Sandro Botticelli's [The Birth of Venus](/birth-of-venus/), Titian's Venus of Urbino, and Raphael's School of Athens, already covered above through its surviving cartoon. Leonardo, Michelangelo and Raphael are usually grouped as the High Renaissance's three central figures, while Botticelli represents the earlier Florentine Renaissance and Titian the later Venetian school.

Renaissance works dominate almost every version of this list. The three that recur most consistently across surveys and museum-attendance figures are Da Vinci's Mona Lisa at the Louvre, his The Last Supper in Milan, and Michelangelo's [Sistine Chapel ceiling](/michelangelo-sistine-chapel/) at the Vatican. No single museum or scholarly body ranks them by number, but all three combine instant public recognition with more than 500 years of continuous documentation, a combination almost no work from any other period matches.

before_faq: They are two different ceramic techniques that share a borrowed name. Maiolica (with an i) refers to the tin-glazed process used in Renaissance Italy and earlier in Spain: an opaque white tin glaze is painted directly with pigment before a single firing sets both together. Majolica (with a j) usually refers to the English technique that came after, developed by Leon Arnoux for Minton starting in 1849, in which saturated lead glazes are fired onto molded, relief-decorated earthenware. As the V&A's own catalogue entry for Minton's ware puts it, quoted above, the resemblance is glaze color described as \"inspired by\" Italian tones, not a return to the older tin-glaze method itself.

It comes from Majorca, the island through which Spanish wares passed en route to Italy, not where anything was actually made. Wares made using this process in Valencia made their way to Italy starting around 1400, routed through Majorca along the way. Buyers in Italy began referring to the imported ware, and eventually to their homegrown versions of it too, by the name of that transshipment point rather than the actual Spanish production towns of Malaga and Valencia.

Leon Arnoux, who trained as a ceramic chemist in France at Sevres, moved to Stoke-on-Trent in 1848 and went to work for Herbert Minton, developing the saturated lead-based glazes behind the pottery line's name. The finished pottery debuted at London's 1851 world's fair, first marketed as \"Palissy ware,\" honoring Bernard Palissy, the French potter whose naturalistic glazed reliefs inspired Arnoux, before the name \"majolica\" took over as the standard term for the same product.

Istoriato, meaning \"storied\" in Italian, describes the Italian tin-glazed ware, discussed above, when painted with full narrative scenes, mythological, historical, or biblical, covering an entire dish or plate instead of simple border ornament or heraldry. It became the signature achievement of Italian maiolica workshops in centers including Urbino, Deruta, Faenza, and Gubbio, taking hold as the 1500s began. Xanto, active in Urbino from 1530 and introduced above, is the artist most historians point to first when discussing istoriato ware, thanks to how often he put his name and a date on his surviving pieces.

Treat it as decorative rather than functional. Because 19th-century majolica relies on lead-based glazes, and the UK's first legal solubility limits on those glazes did not take effect until 1950, under the regulation detailed above, older pieces predating enforceable limits can leach lead, particularly with acidic foods or drinks. The Center for Environmental Health advises that vintage and antique ceramics made before modern lead standards took hold should generally be reserved for display rather than eating or drinking use.

Look at the glaze, the weight, and the underside. Genuine period pieces are heavy, thickly potted, and finished with rich, saturated colors and detailed relief modeling; the unglazed foot ring should show the raw clay body rather than glaze. Fine surface crazing is a sign of real age rather than a flaw, while a piece in flawless, unblemished condition is more likely a modern reproduction, and a maker's mark helps but isn't required, since plenty of genuine 19th-century pieces left the factory unmarked.

Yes, though prices vary widely by maker, size, and condition. English majolica pieces from makers such as Minton or Wedgwood typically bring several hundred to several thousand dollars each at auction, while French majolica tends to sell for less, often in the low hundreds. Chips, cracks, and heavy restoration all reduce value, though the light crazing common on genuinely old glazes doesn't.

Both, at different points in its history. The tin-glaze technique itself reached Europe through Moorish Spain, where wares from the region around Valencia passed through Majorca en route to Italy, the transshipment point that gave the pottery its name. Later, Italian workshops developed the style further during the Renaissance, adding the brightly painted narrative scenes (istoriato ware) that made maiolica famous, so while the technique's European roots are Spanish and Moorish, its best-known artistic identity is Italian.

Examine the relief, glaze, weight and base together, then compare the form and any factory marks with documented examples. Period ware often has substantial weight and rich colours, but these features alone cannot date it. The Majolica International Society warns about copies, disguised marks and repairs, and notes that undersides are usually glazed. Some genuine examples are unmarked. Crazing deserves a condition check; neither its presence nor a flawless surface establishes authenticity.

Yes, but a maker’s name alone does not establish a price. Form, rarity, size, provenance, damage and repairs all matter. To illustrate the range, Christie’s listed a circa-1870 Minton rotating tray with an estimate of $500–800 and an 1861 Minton Bacchus vase at $1,500–2,000 in its 2023 Rothschild sale. Those are estimates for specific English objects, not sale results or a rule that French majolica must be cheaper. Inspect chips, cracks, restoration and crazing when comparing examples.

before_faq: It is a small panel painting done in tempera and gold, 21.4×16 cm, that William Blake completed around 1819-20 on a board of mahogany-type wood. It shows a hybrid, muscular figure, part man and part reptile, moving between drawn curtains with a bowl of blood in its grip. Tate in London catalogues the panel as N05889, part of its collection of British art.

Blake scholars disagree, and the disagreement runs in a direction that might surprise readers who assume Blake was the one convinced of his own visions. In fact, Keynes argued that John Varley, the astrologer who hosted the sessions and asked Blake to draw them, treated the whole exercise with far more conviction than Blake ever showed, reading Blake's sketches as recall and invention rather than literal sight of a spirit. Kathleen Raine reads it differently, portraying the sessions as an easygoing, informal game where neither man needed the other to share his beliefs for the evenings to work.

In Varley's handwriting, the reverse identifies the subject as the vision of a flea's spirit that appeared to Blake, credits him as the artist behind well-known illustration work, states that the vision kept appearing to Varley himself while Blake worked on the picture, and notes that the flea left blood on the panel. Because the inscription calls Blake already deceased, it must date from after his 1827 death, well past the sessions themselves, making it an after-the-fact caption rather than a contemporary record.

John Varley acquired it around 1820; it passed to his son Albert Varley, who gave it up in February 1878 (a sale corroborated separately by a note left in that sketchbook by William Bell Scott himself, a poet and artist). Sotheby's sold it on 14 July 1892 to a London collector, Robertson, who paid £10.50 and later lent the piece to the Tate starting in 1913. Robertson died in September 1948, leaving it to the nation as a bequest, and Tate's records date the completed gift to the following year, 1949.

It is a proposed source rather than a confirmed one. Blake's flea may echo an existing image: a flea drawn magnified through a lens in a 1665 book by Robert Hooke titled Micrographia. Hope Werness, an art historian, has flagged that engraving as a possible model given how widely the book circulated in Britain. No direct documentary link between Blake and that specific engraving has been established, so it remains a plausible source, not a settled fact about the painting's origin.

before_faq: No single location matches it. Each separate rock feature, the Zirkelstein, the Gamrig, the Kaiserkrone, plus one more peak, the Kaltenberg or possibly the Rosenberg depending on which source you check, together making up the same sandstone range straddling Saxony and Bohemia, and scholarship still hasn't settled which of the pair appears in the painting. Friedrich sketched them separately in the field and then combined them in the studio, following his usual working method, so the view as painted couldn't be seen from any single spot anywhere in that mountain range.

No. It depicts a real spot in Suffolk, the millpond next to the cottage owned by Willy Lott, close to Flatford Mill, but the finished six-foot canvas took shape inside Constable's London studio in 1821. He worked from open-air sketches made the previous year and from a full-scale color study, which the V&A now holds, that he used to work out how everything in the frame would balance ahead of the final canvas.

No. Constable showed it in the Royal Academy's 1821 exhibition as Landscape: Noon, per the museum's own record of the entry. John Fisher, a clergyman and friend of Constable's, coined The Hay Wain sometime later, and that label edged out the original title in public memory.

No. The painting compresses topography from five or more separate climate zones across the Ecuadorean Andes, from tropical jungle to the snow-capped peak of Mount Chimborazo, into a single composed view. Church built it from sketches gathered across two trips, one in 1853 and another in 1857, covering ground in both Colombia and Ecuador, guided by a theory Humboldt himself had put forward, that a landscape could represent a region's full climatic character rather than one real spot.

That specific detail is unverified. before_faq: It's an 1841 oil on canvas by the English Romantic painter John Martin, roughly 123×185 cm, showing the moment Hell's great palace rises up out of the ground, the scene that opens Milton's epic Paradise Lost. It has hung in the Louvre in Paris since 2006, in the Denon wing's room 713, catalogued as RF 2006 21.

Milton coined the word for Paradise Lost, fusing a Greek root meaning \"every\" with a Latin root for demon, then attached it to the fallen angels' council chamber, the capital city they raise for Satan and his lieutenants. That word has drifted far from the poem and now just means uproar or chaos in ordinary English.

No. The 1841 oil was his third version of the scene. He first rendered it in mezzotint in 1824, part of a two-dozen-print series drawn from the poem, issued to subscribers from 1825 to 1827. He engraved a larger, separate print of the same scene again in 1831, before finally painting it in oil in 1841, seventeen years after the first version.

No, though the two are easy to confuse because both illustrate the same building described in Milton's poem. Pandemonium shows Hell's palace from outside; its companion mezzotint from the same 1820s series shows the interior instead, Satan enthroned before the assembled fallen angels. Two English museums holding copies of that interior print, named above, credit it, not the Louvre's oil, with shaping how D.W. Griffith's earliest silent films were staged and, decades later, a Star Wars prequel's council-chamber design.

Per the Louvre's published ownership history, its first owner was Benjamin Hick, a Bolton engineer who built steam locomotives, until his death in 1842, then sold in Manchester at his 1843 estate sale. It stayed within one family, the Whiteleys, across four generations until 1994, then to a collection owned by the Forbes publishing family until a 2003 Christie's sale sent it onward to a New York gallery, and finally to the Louvre in 2006, acquired through the bequest of the French architect Pierre Belliot and his wife.

The Louvre hasn't disclosed what it paid when it acquired the painting in 2006, and as part of a national museum collection, it isn't for sale. As a benchmark, the auction record for any John Martin painting is $4,183,482, set in 2015 at Sotheby's London for its 1841 companion piece described above, a fellow large apocalyptic history painting from the same period.

before_faq: That's disputed. RMFAB has held the piece since 1912, and a 1996 technical study raised serious doubts about the attribution to Bruegel. The museum's position is that the composition is certainly Bruegel's design, likely based on a lost original from around 1558, though the canvas itself is now usually classified as a period copy from an unknown hand. A fresh technical study began in 2026, run with a Belgian cultural-heritage research institute, and aims to clarify the question further, with results planned for a 2028 Bruegel exhibition.
It belongs to RMFAB, in Brussels. As of the 2026 technical study, the painting is off view while conservators complete non-invasive testing, and should return to display in roughly October 2026.

Auden's 1938 poem, written after his December visit to the Brussels museum, is the best-known response to the painting. Williams wrote his own poem sharing the painting's title, published in 1960; it later appeared in his 1962 poetry collection; he received the Pulitzer Prize for it after his death.

Draper, an English painter working in the late-Victorian classical revival style. The Royal Academy showed the painting in 1898, and the Chantrey fund purchased it that same year; two years later it earned a gold medal at the 1900 Paris world's fair, and it now belongs to Tate.

It's a deliberate departure from the myth. Draper kept Icarus's wings fully intact in the painting instead of showing him falling without them, most likely because a winged figure reads as a more symbolic and visually elegant image than an image of a young man falling with no wings left at all.

In Matisse's 1943 cut-out, made for his illustrated book Jazz, Icarus falls through a blue sky dotted with yellow bursts, but Matisse gave him a prominent red heart where the ancient myth blamed hubris for the fall. Scholars reading the work in the context of its creation, during the Nazi occupation of France while members of Matisse's own family were active in the Resistance, connect that red heart to passion and personal danger rather than to punishment for flying too high. Matisse himself described Icarus's fall as happening \"with a passionate heart,\" a phrase that points away from the moralizing usually attached to the myth.

In the underlying Greek myth, the craftsman Daedalus built wings of feathers and wax so he and his son Icarus could escape imprisonment on Crete. Daedalus warned Icarus not to fly too low, where sea spray would weigh the feathers down, or too high, where the sun would melt the wax; Icarus ignored the warning, climbed nearer the sun than his father had allowed, and fell into the sea when his wings failed. Painters have handled the moment very differently ever since: the Bruegel painting central to this page shows the fall as a barely noticed detail in a busy landscape, in keeping with the poem it inspired, while other artists, Matisse included, put Icarus himself front and center.
